P10r: Most institutions get more and more layers and offices as they age. The Zapatistas did a review of theirs, and then pushed authority down. Did they put out a book on leadership and open a certification program? Nope. They just went and changed the system they were actually living in.
P10s: Most institutions get more and more layers and offices as they age, right? But the Zapatistas reviewed theirs and pushed authority down. Did they put out a book on leadership and open a certification program? No, they changed the system they were actually living in.
P13q: Now, the Zapatistas also don't prove my whole economic path. (That's the one that goes from unpriced internal necessities, to a common purse, to getting rid of outside money.) Do their communities use collective work to support their schools and clinics, and their autonomous government and resistance? Yes. But they also sell products and trade, and they get outside support. What they do show is that a community can stop buying major necessities and public functions on the market, and govern them collectively instead. And outside help can make a community more capable, sure, but it can also create gatekeepers and uneven dependence, if the specialist or the donor or the organization stays indispensable.

P17j: Then there's sociocracy, which comes from a very different history but ended up with some similar forms: circles, consent, distributed authority, and links between levels.
